report:
## Conclusion: Yes — There Is Evidence That Olive Leaf Extract Can Reduce High Blood Pressure

Multiple clinical trials and at least two systematic reviews/meta-analyses support the conclusion that olive leaf extract (OLE) can modestly lower both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in pre-hypertensive and hypertensive individuals.

### Key Evidence

1. **2025 Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis** (published in *Phytotherapy Research*): Pooled data showed that olive leaf extract at approximately 1,000 mg/day reduced systolic blood pressure by −11.45 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure by −4.65 mmHg. The authors noted limitations including variable trial quality and called for larger, more comprehensive studies to confirm efficacy and safety. ([Wiley/Phytotherapy Research](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509))

2. **2025 Multicenter RCT** (published in the *Journal of Hypertension*): A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 621 participants found that oral olive leaf extract helped control blood pressure in patients already treated for hypertension. ([J Hypertension](https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/abstract/2025/11000/efficacy_of_olive_leaf_extracts_in_controlling.17.aspx))

3. **Earlier Systematic Review** (IntechOpen, 2022): A prior meta-analysis specifically on the anti-hypertensive effect of OLE confirmed reductions in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure across multiple trials. ([IntechOpen](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/80445))

4. **Mechanism**: The active compound **oleuropein** is believed to lower blood pressure by reducing oxidative stress, enhancing nitric oxide production (which relaxes blood vessels), and possibly inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Memorial Sloan Kettering also notes that animal and human studies confirm blood pressure–lowering effects. ([MSKCC](https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/olive-leaf))

### Caveats
The evidence is promising but not definitive. Trial quality varies, sample sizes in some studies are small, and OLE should not replace prescribed antihypertensive medications without medical supervision. Higher doses (~1,000 mg/day) appear more effective than lower doses.
